title: Does It Matter Which AP Courses You Take?
summary:
Does It Matter Which AP Courses You Take?
Johanna Alonso Wed, 10/21/2026 - 03:00 AM

Six AP courses correlated with an admissions advantage, according to data from a college counseling company. It’s unclear whether those courses led to the boost or if confounding variables played a role.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
A study of more than 11,700 college applicants found that only six particular Advanced Placement courses correlate with a noteworthy college admissions boost, while another six appear to have no impact on whether students get into colleges.

The study, conducted by college consulting company Empowerly using a database of the firm’s clients, found that Calculus BC—the second of two AP Calculus courses—appeared to have the biggest impact, increasing a student’s likelihood of admission by 5.2 percent compared to students with a comparable GPA who hadn’t taken the class. The other AP courses that appeared to help were psychology (+4.6 percent), biology (+4.6 percent), chemistry (+4.5 percent), English language (+4 percent) and statistics (+3.2 percent). The data dates back to 2021.

Other courses were associated with significant boosts but lacked a large enough sample size to know for sure, according to the report. Those include comparative government, which only 85 students in the database took, but which appeared to increase a student’s chance of admission by a massive 32.7 percent. Only 34 students took AP Latin, but students in that group were 22.1 percent more likely to be admitted.

With the report, Empowerly aimed to better understand which AP courses are most valuable for getting into selective colleges. Most selective institutions consider course rigor in their admissions decisions, though most take into account that not all AP courses are available at every school. But the question about which and how many AP courses students should take to find the most success in the admissions process is a complex one that varies from institution to institution.

The topic “comes up every single year,” said Empowerly founder Changxiao Xie, “because whenever families are going through course selection, they always have to ask the question, ‘Which courses should I take? What courses are going to help impact admissions, especially around my major?’”

Those decisions can also have high stakes for students’ academic success; students who feel pressure to take too many AP courses could sacrifice other opportunities or end up in courses they can’t pass. Trevor Packer, who leads the AP program for College Board, told EdWeek in 2023 that between 2 and 3 percent of high schoolers take “large” numbers of AP courses.

“Our own research shows that is not necessary for college readiness,” he said. “Simply taking one or two AP classes at most per year of high school optimizes the type of college readiness that comes from taking that type of challenging class.”

But historically, it has been difficult to understand the impact of specific AP classes on admissions because that data isn’t readily available. That’s why the staff at Empowerly decided to use their own data to study the issue.

The report acknowledges that the correlation doesn’t necessarily mean that these classes directly caused more students to be admitted. The research doesn’t control for other possible confounding variables, such as whether students who took courses like Calculus BC also took a higher number of AP courses in general—though Empowerly told Inside Higher Ed the company hopes to dive further into how the number of AP courses affects admissions in the future.

Stephanie Owen, an economics professor at Colby College who has studied AP courses, said she wouldn’t draw significant conclusions from the report about the impact of individual courses on admissions.

“There are reasons why we would think that certain subjects might matter more in admissions than others. It could be that they are signaling certain abilities of students; it could be that admissions officers are trying to balance across majors,” she said. “I think it’s something it would be nice to know more about, but, unfortunately, I don’t think this report tells us that for sure. But I think it’s definitely worth looking into more.”

Past research on the impacts of the AP program has been mixed, Owen said. Students who pass AP exams are more likely to graduate college on time, indicating that the program is meeting its goal of helping students get through college faster by skipping some general education courses. But it’s not as clear whether students who take the course but don’t take or pass the exam see those benefits. In her own research, Owen found that adding one extra AP course to a school did result in the most high-achieving students going to four-year schools at higher rates. The majority of students didn’t see a boost, though.

Empowerly’s findings also have implications for equity in admissions; just 33 percent of schools offer Calculus BC, the course correlated with the biggest admissions boost. Calculus AB, which is more common, was not correlated with such a bump.

title: Poll: Battleground Voters Oppose Political Control of Grant Making
summary:
Poll: Battleground Voters Oppose Political Control of Grant Making
kathryn.palmer… Wed, 10/21/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Kathryn Palmer
full_text:
Ahead of the midterm elections Nov. 3, a new poll shows that voters in some Midwestern battleground states don’t approve of the federal government’s plans to assert more political control over the federal grant-making process.

Earlier this month, United for Cures Action surveyed 1,200 registered voters in Iowa, Kansas, and Ohio, all of which Republican President Donald Trump won in 2024. According to the survey, published last week, 76 percent of voters in those states oppose the Office of Management and Budget’s proposal to overhaul the grant-approval process, including at the National Institutes of Health, the National Science Foundation and other federal agencies that send millions in research funding to universities each year. Right now, peer reviewers at those agencies make the final decision on who is awarded a grant. But under the proposal (which advocacy groups, including United for Cures, have opposed), political appointees would have the final say on awards, which could be canceled at their discretion.

Strong voter opposition to the proposal extends across geographic and party lines. According to the poll, 77 percent of voters in Iowa and Kansas oppose, along with 75 percent in Ohio. Across all three states, 88 percent of Democrats, 82 percent of independents and 64 percent of Republicans oppose it.

The poll also found that 64 percent believe the federal government spends too little on medical research, while 91 percent believe that federally funded medical research has had a “great deal” or “some” impact on finding breakthrough cures and treatments.

The “bottom line,” United for Cures Action wrote in a memo about the poll, is “Voters clearly do not want increased political interference with federal grants from EITHER party.”

title: The Shils Report and Academic Merit
summary:
The Shils Report and Academic Merit
Sara Brady Wed, 10/21/2026 - 03:00 AM

It’s not a triumphant monument to academic merit, but an attack that seeks to purge leftist faculty.

Byline(s)
John K. Wilson
full_text:
Hundreds of colleges have adopted the University of Chicago’s 1967 Kalven report and the 2014 Chicago principles as part of national campaigns led by the Foundationfor Individual Rights and Expression, the American Council of Trustees and Alumni, the Academic Freedom Alliance, and Heterodox Academy. But the largely ignored part of the so-called Chicago Trifecta, the 1970 Shils report, has never been copied by another university.

In a recent Chronicle of Higher Education essay, Dean Saitta points to the Shils report as “especially germane in the current moment of disciplinary self-reflection and soul-searching.” Germane, yes. A desirable model, not so much. The Shils report actually represents the betrayal of academic merit in order to get rid of troublesome left-wing faculty—so it’s no surprise that it is increasingly invoked by conservatives today when this political purge is the explicit goal of too many politicians and leaders.

Some admirers of the Shils report seem to imagine that its lead author, sociologist Edward Shils, invented the concept of academic merit. In reality, academic merit was already always and everywhere the presumed norm for academic hiring, albeit often violated in practice. So the statements about academic merit in the Shils report were just standard university blather. The primary innovation of the Shils report was to identify an exception to academic merit for leftist political activists in order to purge progressives from the University of Chicago.

In addition to teaching and research, the Shils report invents a new third aspect of academic evaluation: “contribution to intellectual community.” And the report explicitly downplays service on academic committees as having any importance. Instead, this criterion included vague standards about “conversation in informal situations,” designed to favor the men who discussed ideas over lunch at the Quadrangle Club. But the key part of the “intellectual community” standard is what deserved a negative evaluation that seemed designed to be absolute and disqualifying: “They will abstain from deliberate disruption of the regular operations of the University.” These disruptive protests, according to the Shils report, “cannot claim the protection of academic freedom” and therefore justify purging leftist faculty who embrace them.

(The Shils report does include a fourth criterion, “services,” which mostly applies to medical professors, but it otherwise dismisses the idea of service except for the positive value of editing an academic journal.)

As Saitta points out, the primary motivation for the appointment of the committee that delivered the Shils report was the controversy over sociology professor Marlene Dixon being denied reappointment shortly after she defiantly stood with student protesters against the university administration. The campus protests and sit-in against Dixon’s firing led to one of the largest mass expulsions of student protesters on an American campus and were followed by a dramatic decline in student enrollment that took decades for the University of Chicago to recover from.

But Dixon was not the only leftist sociology professor denied tenure by Shils and his colleagues. A few months after Dixon’s tenure denial roiled the Chicago campus, antiwar professor Richard Flacks (who had already been denied tenure the year before and was serving out his terminal year) was almost beaten to death in his office on May 5, 1969, by an unknown assailant posing as a reporter who wanted to talk with him about his activism. The FBI later denied any involvement in the attack—which may seem like a strange thing for the FBI to do, until you find out that the FBI had launched a covert campaign to have Flacks fired by having an agent pose as a concerned parent writing to the trustees to ask them to remove Flacks. This FBI subterfuge seems like an almost comical misunderstanding of university affairs, where the trustees would never intervene and faculty like Shils would make sure they never needed to, by getting rid of the leftist professors themselves.

Cases like Flacks and Dixon alarmed Shils. He could easily dismiss Marxist academic work, and did so in a report he wrote for the committee that examined Dixon’s case. Denying tenure or reappointment to leftist radicals was easy enough to do, but the protests that resulted could tear apart the campus. Shils wanted to solve this problem by making participation in left-wing protests and sit-ins a reason to ban faculty from being appointed in the first place. There would be no campus protests against tenure denials of faculty like Dixon because the left-wing activists would never get hired.

The murky waters of hiring decisions make it hard to determine to what extent the Shils report has influenced academic appointments at the University of Chicago. Did the “deliberate disruption” rule actually cause any faculty committee to reject hiring a leftist professor? We will probably never know.

Many times, the Shils report violates norms of academic merit and seeks special preferences for traditional, conservative viewpoints: “Great caution must be exercised by appointive committees themselves to prevent their being ‘stampeded’ by the prestige or influence of contemporaneity.” The delusion that there was a “stampede” to embrace new ideas at the University of Chicago is rather laughable.

The Shils report warned of “an increasing tendency for universities to concern themselves in their teaching and research with contemporary events—especially in the social sciences and Humanities.” Shils wanted the university to have an explicit bias against current events, regardless of the academic merit of that research, because he correctly perceived it as a path for more liberal ideas to enter academia.

The Shils report was guilty of what it warns against: “contemporaneity.” It was an overreaction to a contentious moment in campus history when people feared that the core of the University of Chicago was being torn apart from within. And in response, conservatives like Shils made the mistake of straying from academic merit in order to provide an opportunity to get rid of leftists who might engage in “deliberate disruption.”

In the years since it was written, everyone has assumed that the Shils report must be a tribute to academic merit. A 2022 statement by Stanford-affiliated faculty on “Restoring Academic Freedom” called for all universities to adopt the Chicago Trifecta, including “the Shils report making academic contribution the sole basis for hiring and promotion.“ University of Chicago professor Dorian Abbot wrote, “The Shils report requires that faculty hiring and promotion be done solely on the basis of research and teaching merit, with nothing else taken into consideration.” But the Shils report did precisely the opposite of making research and teaching merit the “sole basis” for academic appointments by including the third criterion of “intellectual community” and making anything deemed “deliberate disruption” justification for discrimination.

Some advocates of the Shils report imagine that colleges reject it because of the provision prohibiting considerations of race, gender or other irrelevant characteristics. In reality, nondiscrimination statements were commonplace by the time of the Shils report, and they were completely compatible with calls for affirmative action and diversity. The question of whether you best achieve nondiscrimination by pretending to ignore race or by being aware of its potential biases is still hotly contested, but both approaches work with the words of the Shils report.

Ironically, it’s likely that the Shils report (unlike the Kalven report and the Chicago principles) will never be adopted by any university (and probably is ignored in practice even at the University of Chicago) because it is too left-wing.

The real reason why the Shils report won’t be adopted by universities is because of an academic value much more fundamental than diversity: money. While those largely symbolic and ignored diversity statements are on the wane, colleges increasingly focus on a more important faculty attribute: the ability to lure funding. Candidates for hiring and tenure alike have demands placed on them to display a strong record of attracting external grants, and these profitability statements have become entrenched in academia.

Shils’s old-fashioned conservatism included resentment at the growing corporatization of universities in the 1960s, where government funding of science had fueled a new wave of investment. The Shils report declared that “the capacity or incapacity of a candidate to attract financial resources or to ‘bring them with him’ should not be a criterion for appointment” and warned, “If this rule is not observed, the University will be in danger of becoming an aggregate of affluent mediocrities “ That’s a bold principle—one far too dangerous for universities devoted to the pursuit of affluence.

The Shils report is not a terrible document. The wise warning about “affluent mediocrities” is extraordinary, and most of its routine details about academic merit are quite thoughtful. A few elements positively reflect the progressive impulses of the time, such as “inviting and considering the assessments of candidates for appointment made in a consultative capacity by students.” But its beneficial elements are almost certain to be ignored, while its dangerous willingness to amend academic merit in order to remove “disruptive” professors might be its primary appeal today (along with the mistaken belief that its standard ban on racial discrimination would prohibit affirmative action).

The Shils report is not a triumphant monument to academic merit that needs to be imitated by other universities; it is an attack on academic merit that seeks to purge leftist faculty for their protests.

title: Faisal Islam: Inflation and borrowing figures illustrate chancellor's Budget challenge
summary: The economic figures released on Wednesday show the constraints for John Healey as he puts the finishing touches to his Budget.
full_text:
The chancellor was on an early flight to North East Scotland on Wednesday to announce new North Sea energy approvals as the last set of major economic figures dropped.

From a mile high, as well as close up, the figures for inflation and for the public finances set out his Budget balancing act in clear terms.

The National Debt has topped £3 trillion for the first time in the official figures.

The headline rate of inflation has hit 3.5% and is surely heading back up to 4% in the coming months.

Borrowing is running ahead of forecasts, as spending and interest costs increase.

These show the constraints for John Healey as he puts the finishing touches to his statement next week.

On the one hand he says he wants to give "breathing space" to consumers yet again feeling the heat from cost of living pressures.

The public finances remain under pressure, however, from the double whammy of rising inflation and borrowing costs.

While inflation was of course expected to increase as petrol and diesel prices surged, in some cases, to records, other measures of underlying inflation also increased.

From airfares to computer game download prices, there are the first signs of stickier forms of price pressure and of higher inflation becoming more embedded, suggesting elevated price rises are not temporary. Capital Economics now expects the main measure of inflation to peak at 4.2% next year.

The Bank of England carefully watches services inflation and core inflation, and this ups the odds significantly for a rise in interest rates next month.

The services sector, which includes everything from law and banking to retail, hospitality and tourism, makes up the vast majority of the UK's economic output.

title: ‘Evil man will be punished’: Rijiju warns Delhi man over racial abuse of Tripura youth
full_text:
From Rijiju to Tripura opposition, outrage over alleged racial abuse of tribal youth

NEW DELHI: Union minister Kiren Rijiju late Wednesday strongly condemned "racial" harassment of a tribal youth from Tripura's Gomati district by a Delhi-based social media influencer Amir Shokeen. Rijiju took to X and shared a video of the incident, acknowledging the delay in filing an official complaint but warning that the accused would face action. "This evil man will be punished. There was delay in lodging the official complaint but Delhi Police and Tripura Police will teach him a hard lesson. People who tolerate such wicked behavior in the society are also responsible for the spread of hatred," the Union parliamentary affairs minister said. In the video circulating online, Shokeen can allegedly be heard making racial remarks against the youth. The clip, which surfaced on Tuesday evening, purportedly shows him asking the young man whether he was the "president" of a neighbouring country. He allegedly mocked Tripura when the youth responded that he was Indian. Political parties in Tripura closed ranks on Wednesday over the incident and demanded legal action against Shokeen. Tripura chief minister Manik Saha directed the state director general of police to coordinate with Delhi Police and ensure a proper investigation into the incident. CPM state secretary and leader of the opposition Jitendra Chaudhury demanded an apology from Shokeen. "Establish a precedent that is both resounding and unmistakable, ensuring no one ever dares insult Tripura and the Tiprasa community again," he said.

title: New Zealand to help more schools recruit international students
summary:
New Zealand is investing up to NZ$2.5 million in a new support service designed to help more schools recruit, enrol and retain international students from 2027, as the government pushes ahead with ambitious international education growth targets.

The post New Zealand to help more schools recruit international students appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Education minister Erica Stanford said the initiative would target both schools with established international programs and those that have struggled to enter the market.

“This support is not limited to schools that already have well-established international programs,” said Stanford.

“We want more schools to benefit from the opportunities international education offers, while continuing to build capability across the school sector.”

Education New Zealand (ENZ) has selected academyEX as the preferred provider following a competitive tender process. Its contract begins in October 2026, with ENZ overseeing implementation.

Around 611 New Zealand schools currently enrol international students, but the government said participation remains constrained by a range of practical barriers.

These include limited capacity and expertise in international recruitment, enrolment and student support, difficulties developing overseas networks and challenges securing homestay accommodation.

Under the new service, schools will be offered tools, templates and resources alongside training, coaching and advisory support covering the international student journey.

The program will be tailored to individual institutions, with support available to schools recruiting international students for the first time as well as those seeking to grow established programs.

academyEX will also work with international education stakeholders and draw on expertise already present within schools, with the aim of encouraging institutions to learn from each other.

International students enrich our schools and communities by bringing new perspectives, cultures and global connections, helping prepare young people for an increasingly connected world

Erica Stanford, education minister

“International students enrich our schools and communities by bringing new perspectives, cultures and global connections, helping prepare young people for an increasingly connected world,” said Stanford.

The government is also pitching wider participation in international education as a way to spread its benefits beyond schools that already have mature international operations, with more communities expected to benefit from student spending as well as cultural and educational exchange.

The initiative forms part of New Zealand’s International Education Going for Growth Plan, under which the government is targeting 105,000 international student enrolments by 2027 and NZ$7.2 billion in export earnings from the sector by 2034.

“Our job now is to keep the momentum going by backing education providers to grow and helping more communities benefit from the economic, cultural and educational value international students bring,” said Stanford.

full_text:
Higher education’s reliance on third-party software and Software as a Service platforms has never been more consequential. Recent attacks on learning management systems and other platforms used by higher education institutions have demonstrated how a vulnerability at a technology provider can become a problem for institutions that depend on it.

For universities, the challenge is particularly acute. Third-party applications are embedded in teaching, research, administration and student services, often handling enormous amounts of sensitive data. How can institutions take advantage of these technologies without assuming that a trusted vendor is necessarily a secure one? How do they assess risk, balance security with the need for innovation, monitor vendors after deployment and prepare for the possibility that a compromise somewhere in the software ecosystem could ultimately affect their institutions?

EdTech spoke with Jon Allen, associate vice president, CIO and CISO at Baylor University; Fred Kwong, vice president and CISO at DeVry University; and Shefali Mookencherry, CISO and chief privacy officer at the University of Illinois Chicago, to learn how they’re managing risk at their institutions.

WATCH: A CDW webinar outlines how to map third-party SaaS risk.

HEALTHTECH: Jon, you were there when higher education institutions began collaborating more to assess the security risks of third-party software. Set the stage for us.

Allen: Back when higher ed started getting serious about cloud applications — and security reviews around cloud applications — it was a nightmare. Every institution had its own questionnaire for each vendor. If they were lucky, they got it back in 30 days. In all likelihood, it was filled out by a salesperson, not somebody who actually knew the environment. And it was hard to produce quality assessments.

At the 2016 EDUCAUSE cybersecurity conference, we asked, “Why aren’t we collaborating as institutions?” Originally, the idea was shared assessments, but that’s hard. Institutions have different risk postures, and vendors weren’t keen on institutions sharing detailed assessments with each other. So, we created the Higher Education Community Vendor Assessment Toolkit. That was a big evolution in the higher ed space.

Often, I’ll now engage with a vendor, and they’ll give me a completed HECVAT. It may not always be the most up-to-date version, but it’s not like starting from zero. We have a common language. We have common expectations.

LEARN MORE: Third-party risk management helps institutions detect threats.

HEALTHTECH: Considering recent breaches among software providers, how would you characterize the current threat environment?

Mookencherry: Universities must be more vigilant than ever in monitoring and managing risk. Third-party breaches are occurring with increasing frequency and receiving greater public attention, while regulatory requirements continue to expand. Encouragingly, third-party organizations are becoming more aware of their compliance obligations and are being held to higher standards of accountability than in the past. As security programs mature nationally and globally, transparency and visibility into cyber risks have increased significantly. The era when organizations could assume they were unlikely to experience a breach is behind us. For higher education institutions, risk assessment can no longer be a periodic exercise; it must be a continuous and ongoing process.

Kwong: I would say it’s a higher-risk environment than what we’ve seen in the past. Threat actors can leverage artificial intelligence to discover vulnerabilities, find flaws and execute against them. Before, sophisticated threat actors had the skill sets to do those things; now it’s in the hands of the masses. And that’s the scary part.

Allen: What constitutes risk at this point? Five years ago, everybody would have said Social Security numbers, credit card numbers, things like that — data elements. But at the end of the day, if core business or academic applications are unavailable, that can almost be more catastrophic to your operation than data loss, which is a sad situation.

We’re starting to get a hint of the new threat landscape under AI and various geopolitical tensions. It’s a contentious time, from that standpoint. The next 12 to 18 months are going to be hard.

HEALTHTECH: How has your approach to evaluating third-party software changed over the past few years?

Mookencherry: As part of every software contract renewal, universities should conduct a comprehensive reassessment of vendor risk to account for evolving threats, emerging technologies and ongoing innovation. Universities should typically require vendors to provide a SOC 2 Type II report or a HECVAT assessment, when available. If those certifications are not yet in place, the university should work collaboratively with the vendor to establish a roadmap and timeline for achieving them. If contractual agreements do not clearly define breach notification requirements, response obligations or accountability measures, universities should ensure those provisions are incorporated. Ultimately, the focus is not only on security and compliance but also on strengthening business resilience and ensuring operational continuity in the face of evolving risks.

Kwong: From a questionnaire and assessment perspective, we do it on a yearly basis. We also leverage Bitsight to do continuous monitoring of vendors. It’s a data point that we can use to help us understand if their security posture changes in any significant ways over the course of that year. When we combine those two things together, it gives us a more holistic view of the vendor.

Allen: With many of our regular vendors, we’ll ask them to show us their SOC report or tell us how they handle their cloud environment, and they’ll toss us a Microsoft Azure, AWS or Google Cloud document. But we’re not contracting with those guys — the vendors are. And things can change at any point. We want to see a clear responsibility matrix.

DISCOVER: Continuous threat exposure management helps higher ed prioritize risk.

HEALTHTECH: How do you balance enabling innovation for faculty and staff with maintaining appropriate security oversight?

Mookencherry: Universities thrive on innovation, research, experimentation and academic freedom. The objective is to ensure that security enables these activities rather than impedes them. The goal is not simply to say no. Instead, it is good to understand the risks, establish appropriate safeguards and create a framework that allows universities to confidently say yes.

Experience has shown that when security is perceived as a barrier, users may seek alternative ways to accomplish their objectives. That is why education, awareness and collaboration are critical components of our approach. Working closely with faculty and staff to help them understand potential risks and implement mitigating controls is key. In situations where a higher level of risk is accepted, there may be a requirement for a formal risk acceptance process to ensure that stakeholders understand and acknowledge their responsibilities. The focus is on helping users make informed decisions while identifying practical ways to reduce risk, such as network segmentation, limiting access to authorized users or implementing additional security controls. Ultimately, security’s role is to support innovation while maintaining an appropriate balance between opportunity, risk and institutional resilience.

Allen: We make decisions about implementation based on our assessments. That’s where a lot of risk mitigation happens. We may choose not to put certain data elements into a solution because of what we discovered through an assessment. We may change the way we handle authentication. Those are very campus-oriented decisions based on a risk profile. I’m not saying, “Shame on you, you shouldn’t be using that provider” or, “Hey, you’re not using the right version of TLS.” Instead, we’ll have conversations and educate users about risk.

Mookencherry: Universities should enhance their security assessment questionnaires and vendor review processes to address the growing use of AI. AI concerns center on data oversharing and data leakage. When AI capabilities are embedded within a software solution, it is good to seek a clear understanding of how the vendor manages and protects data, particularly if customer information is used to train, tune or improve AI models.

Given that vendors often serve multiple clients, it is critical to understand how data is segregated, protected and prevented from being exposed across tenant environments. It is good to also assess the vendor’s policies and technical safeguards related to their own AI development and usage practices. Ultimately, there should be assurances that appropriate governance, security, privacy and data protection controls are in place to safeguard institutional information while enabling the benefits of AI-driven innovation.

Kwong: Vetting the AI technologies that vendors are putting in place has been the biggest change to our assessments. Previously, through our vendor management process, we would ask questions about their security posture. Now we’re asking, “What type of AI are you using? How is it being leveraged? How is our data being used, if at all? Is it confined within our own instance or is it combined with other people’s data into a separate instance?”

Interestingly, new vendors are easier to get a handle on. It’s the ones we already have relationships with that suddenly turn on AI and you don’t know about it until you find out either through the grapevine or as part of annual security recertification.

UP NEXT: Are you ready for third-party risk? This checklist can help you be certain.

HEALTHTECH: Looking ahead three to five years, what do you think will be the biggest challenge in managing third-party cyber risk?

Mookencherry: The biggest challenge is visibility. As AI vendors rapidly evolve through startups, mergers and acquisitions, understanding third- and fourth-party risks becomes increasingly difficult. Greater transparency from vendors about both their strengths and gaps would help universities better assess and manage risk. Today, much of that due diligence burden falls on the institution.

Kwong: I think you may see a turnaround for some organizations, especially those that went 100% cloud, where they bring some applications back in-house. That could be particularly true with AI, when they start understanding the token costs of using these third-party models.

There needs to be an AI security framework. We’re all learning this stuff as quickly as possible, and there are various models to work from. But because we have all these vendors working with the technology, they’re in a much better spot to give us insight into how they’re controlling for it. If they could provide that data back out to us, we could look at our own programs and leverage it to be more secure. Being more transparent would help.

title: The next decade of transnational education (TNE): opportunities, challenges and strategic questions for higher education globally
summary: The post The next decade of transnational education (TNE): opportunities, challenges and strategic questions for higher education globally appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Ahead of our Member Benefit event, ‘Leading across university departments, schools and colleges in global engagement and transnational education’, Professor Mark O’Hara says TNE and GE have moved from the margins to being a near ubiquitous feature of institutional strategies.

Transnational education (TNE) and global engagement (GE) have moved from the margins of some university activity to being a near ubiquitous feature of institutional strategies. Once viewed primarily as mechanisms for international student recruitment or partnership development, they are now increasingly central to how universities pursue their educational, economic and societal missions. As higher education enters a period of profound global change, leaders and practitioners involved in TNE / GE will face a series of opportunities, challenges and strategic dilemmas that are likely to shape the sector over the next decade.

One of those trends is the growing shift from isolated international projects towards a desire for more integrated global operating models. Many universities are seeking to connect international partnerships, branch campuses, research collaborations, student mobility programmes and collaborative online international learning (COIL) provision within a single strategic framework. While this offers opportunities for greater coherence and efficiency, it also creates new leadership challenges. Institutions will need leaders capable of working across multiple cultures, knowledgeable about digital / blended pedagogies, regulatory environments and organisational structures, whilst able to balance local responsiveness with institutional priorities.

Alongside increasing integration comes growing complexity. Universities are operating in an increasingly uncertain geopolitical environment characterised by changing diplomatic relationships and outright warfare, as well as shifting patterns of student mobility, economic volatility and evolving immigration policies. Decisions that once appeared straightforward can now carry significant strategic and reputational risk. Institutions must therefore develop the capacity to anticipate and respond to external change while maintaining stable, sustainable international partnerships alongside their duty of care to students, staff and communities.

Questions of regulation and policy are also likely to become more prominent. Governments around the world are paying closer attention to the quality, oversight and strategic implications of cross-border higher education. Regulatory frameworks continue to evolve, often at different speeds and in different directions. Universities engaged in TNE / GE will need to navigate increasingly complex requirements therefore all-the-while remaining aligned with both national priorities and institutional objectives. Understanding how policy environments can enable or constrain international activity will become an important leadership capability in its own right.

At the same time, the rapidly expanding range of partnership models presents its own affordances and conundrums. Traditional arrangements based on programme delivery are increasingly being supplemented by joint institutes, international branch campuses, collaborative research centres, dual awards, online partnerships and blended/hybrid delivery models. As partnerships become more diverse, universities will need to think carefully about accountability and shared ownership. Determining how governance responsibilities are distributed between partners and how institutional values and standards are maintained across different contexts will remain a critical concern therefore.

Quality assurance and enhancement (QAE) will remain, as ever, a major area of focus. While students rightly expect comparable academic experiences regardless of where they study, delivering consistency across different countries and educational systems is not always straightforward. Universities must balance standardisation with flexibility, ensuring that programmes remain responsive to local contexts while maintaining academic integrity. The challenges will not simply be those associated with compliance but will involve the generation of cultures of continuous enhancement that place student learning and success at their heart. This student experience dimension is likely to undergo significant transformation. As TNE / GE expands, institutions will need to consider how best to support increasingly diverse student populations studying across multiple locations, cultures and modes of delivery. Questions around belonging, inclusion, wellbeing, employability and student voice will become ever more important. Universities will need to ensure that internationalisation benefits students not only academically but also socially, culturally and professionally.

Workforce capability and capacity-building will run in parallel with student experience. Delivering successful TNE requires a wide range of expertise extending far beyond academic staff alone. Professional services colleagues, administrators, quality specialists, partnership managers and other ‘third-space’ professionals all play vital roles in supporting international activity. Universities will increasingly need to invest in staff development, intercultural competence and leadership capacity if they are to sustain high-quality international provision over the long term.

As if all this were insufficient, technology will also, without doubt, play its own increasingly influential role. Advances in artificial intelligence, digital learning platforms, learning analytics and virtual collaboration tools are likely to reshape how international education is delivered and experienced. While these developments offer exciting possibilities for expanding access and strengthening collaboration, they also raise important questions around ethics, equity, data protection, academic integrity and digital inclusion. The institutions that thrive will be those that view technology not as a substitute for partnership and human connection, but as a means of enhancing them.

Finally, and perhaps the most significant question facing the sector, concerns the purpose of TNE / GE itself. Increasingly, universities are being challenged to move beyond transactional (income-generation led) approaches towards models based on genuine collaboration, reciprocity and mutual benefit. Partners, students and governments alike are asking whether international activities contribute to broader goals such as social inclusion, sustainable development, knowledge exchange and global citizenship. Institutions will need to consider not simply whether internationalisation can be expanded, but how it can be made more ethical, inclusive and mutually impactful for all those involved.

The next decade therefore promises significant change for those working in transnational education and global engagement. While the opportunities are substantial, so too are the strategic, operational and ethical questions that accompany them. Success will depend upon effective leadership, robust governance, thoughtful policy engagement, strong partnerships and sustained investment in people. For those colleagues interested in exploring these issues in greater depth, exchanging ideas with peers and reflecting on emerging international trends, we invite you to join the forthcoming collaborative webinar programme led by the UK’s Advance-HE, UUKi and QAA teams, on transnational education and global engagement in higher education.

Professor Mark O’Hara is Advance HE’s Senior Consultant, Educational Excellence

For our educational attainment metric, we’re using the percentage of adults (25 and older) with a bachelor’s degree or higher.

The data come from the Census Bureau’s 2020–2024 QuickFacts estimates.

The Census Bureau’s definition of educational attainment is the highest level of schooling or degree completed by an individual, so it doesn’t necessarily reflect skills gained through training programs or on-the-job training. This metric is also distinct from data on who’s currently in school.1

We also looked at high school attainment rates to give a sense of where patterns differ.

Alaska’s Department of Labor and Workforce Development offers Adult Education programs including distance education, English as a Second Language, GED preparation, math, reading, and workplace education.4 These programs help prepare Alaskans for success in the workplace, in a trade or vocational program, or in continuing their education.

Un progetto per la nautica del Sud che riguardi «attività di internazionalizzazione, portualità turistica, sostenibilità e formazione delle competenze». Sono i temi che verranno trattati, tre l’altro, nel corso dello Snim, il Salone nautico di Puglia 2026, che si apre oggi a Marina di Brindisi e proseguirà fino al 26 ottobre; a snocciolare i punti che saranno al centro del piano, e verranno illustrati nel corso del Forum delle imprese nautiche del Mezzogiorno, che si terrà il 23 ottobre, è Giuseppe Meo, presidente dello Snim.

La 22° edizione del boat show mette in mostra 180 espositori e oltre 300 imbarcazioni distribuite su 20mila metri quadrati. E le riflessioni di Meo partono da dati industriali molto concreti: «Il Sud ha cantieri e competenze che devono poter crescere. Secondo il rapporto La nautica in cifre di Confindustria nautica, la Puglia conta 69 infrastrutture portuali e oltre 11mila posti barca. Il XIV Rapporto nazionale sull’economia del mare 2026, a cura di Centro Studi Tagliacarne–Unioncamere e OsserMare, conferma, peraltro il ruolo centrale del Mezzogiorno nell’economia del mare: genera il 34,2% del valore aggiunto diretto nazionale del comparto, pari a circa 27 miliardi di euro, e concentra il 39,9% dell’occupazione, cioè oltre 452mila addetti».

Il Mezzogiorno d’Italia, prosegue Meo, «ha un peso davvero importante per la cantieristica: produce soprattutto barche fino a 15 metri, quella che viene definita “piccola nautica”. Bisogna chiarire, però, la percentuale di produzione di questo tipo di natanti rappresenta l’80% di quella nazionale. Ed è concentrata appunto tra Puglia, Calabria, Campania e Sicilia. Da qui l’idea di lanciare il Progetto Sud, perché in meridione oggi abbiamo le condizioni per far crescere ulteriormente il settore, se mai riuscissimo a migliorare la normativa per la realizzazione e l’ampliamento delle marine, per la realizzazione di porti a secco nonché la possibilità di intercettare investimenti importanti. Senza dimenticare che noi siamo, comunque, aree Zes (Zone economiche speciali) e offriamo opportunità di finanziamento importanti, per chi volesse localizzare qui le produzioni. E poi in un momento internazionale così delicato, il Mezzogiorno rappresenta una piattaforma di rilievo al centro del Mediterraneo».

Per quanto riguarda i temi centrali del Progetto Sud, continua Meo, «un punto focale è l’internazionalizzazione delle imprese. L’idea è di trovare strumenti che possano consentire alle nostre aziende di competere meglio sui mercati internazionali. Tutte le principali fiere sono in Nord Italia o in Europa: lo spostamento dei mezzi dal nostro Sud incide oltre tre volte, rispetto ai costi di qualsiasi altro operatore nazionale. Le barche, purtroppo, vanno esposte e le nostre aziende artigianali, che producono unità fino a 15 metri, incontrano veramente grande difficoltà economiche nel muoversi. Intendiamo, quindi, provare a portare le nostre istanze ai tavoli nazionali, con l’obiettivo di trovare misure di sostegno alle imprese del Sud, anche per il trasferimento dei mezzi, attraverso strumenti governativi e delle camere di commercio».

Sulla portualità turistica, aggiunge Meo, «faccio riferimento, per quanto riguarda il Pogetto Sud, anche solo alla mia regione: abbiamo 900 chilometri di costa e credo che possiamo essere una base importante per il charter nautico. D’altro canto, sul versante adriatico siamo transfrontalieri con Paesi che oggi, sul turismo nautico, hanno decisamente cambiato passo. Mi riferisco a Croazia, Montenegro, Grecia e Turchia ma anche all’Albania».
